221: The elbow method compares within-cluster squared error across candidate values of k and looks for diminishing improvement from adding clusters.
A two-component projection can hide structure present in other dimensions. Visual separation in that projection is subjective and need not identify the best k for the full feature space.
PCA explained variance helps choose the number of retained dimensions, not the number of k-means clusters.
t-SNE perplexity controls the neighborhood scale used in visualization. It is not a cluster count and cannot be substituted for k.
An elbow in the SSE curve identifies a useful tradeoff between compact clusters and extra complexity. It is a heuristic, and some datasets have no clear elbow.
222: Maintaining predictive quality requires both a ground-truth-based monitor and an automated, validated retraining workflow.
Pipelines can orchestrate fresh data extraction, training, evaluation, and deployment, replacing repeated manual notebook execution.

Model quality monitoring can compare predictions with observed loan outcomes and publish metrics for an alarm. An integration such as EventBridge and Lambda can start the pipeline when accuracy falls below its threshold.
Predictions alone cannot reveal accuracy without actual outcomes. A custom daily checker and email also leave retraining manual and duplicate managed monitoring functionality.
Manually rerunning the notebook depends on human intervention and does not provide systematic detection or timely retraining.
An ECS task can automate a script, but requires custom workflow, monitoring, and deployment handling instead of using ML-specific orchestration.
223: A systematic residual trend above a price threshold indicates a relationship the current linear model does not capture; changing the functional form can address it.
Uniformly removing observations does not fix the residual pattern and leaves less information for learning the relationship.
Separate models on either side of the apparent price breakpoint can capture different regimes that a single straight-line model misses.
The lower-price region already has residuals near zero. Discarding its data does not correct the systematic high-price errors.
A fixed offset shifts predictions but does not correct the changing residual slope above 50. The error grows with price rather than remaining constant.
Inspecting the data and applying suitable nonlinear features or transformations can let the model represent the threshold-dependent relationship; the isolated outlier also merits inspection.
A nonlinear model can learn the changing response above the breakpoint. Its improvement should be assessed on held-out data rather than assumed from training fit.
224: k-NN classifies using nearby training examples, and dimensionality reduction reduces the representation stored and searched for those examples.
k-NN directly supports neighbor-based classification and identifying similar points. Reducing the feature dimension lowers the memory needed for the neighbor representation.
Early stopping limits training iterations but does not provide a neighbor index or directly reduce the dimensionality of stored examples.
K-means assigns points to cluster centers. It does not directly provide the requested supervised vegetable classification and nearest-example retrieval.
PCA reduces dimensions, but it is not itself a classifier or a nearest-neighbor search algorithm. Another model would still be required.
225: Debugger rules can detect training pathologies and resource underuse, with configured actions to stop an unproductive training job.
Low CPU use can be normal for GPU-bound training. It does not diagnose vanishing gradients or establish that the GPU is underused.
Custom high-resolution metrics and a Lambda analyzer require instrumentation and rule code that the named built-in Debugger rules already provide.

The vanishing-gradient rule targets a possible convergence problem, while LowGPUUtilization targets wasted GPU capacity. Configuring stop actions avoids paying for a long run after a rule detects an actionable issue.
Confusion and feature-importance rules address prediction behavior and feature contribution. They do not directly target the stated gradient-convergence and GPU-utilization concerns.
226: Local SHAP explanations attribute an individual prediction to input features relative to a reference baseline.
XGBoost plot_importance summarizes global split-based importance. It does not explain why one particular customer received a denial.
Debugger can support tensor-based analysis in appropriate training workflows, but retraining only to obtain explanations adds work when the deployed model can be explained directly.

A Clarify explainability job can evaluate the trained model and compute per-customer SHAP contributions against a suitable baseline without retraining it. Clarify availability must be checked for new AWS customers.
Model Monitor's explainability monitoring tracks changes in feature attribution. A direct Clarify explainability job is the simpler fit for explaining individual existing predictions.
227: Distribution distances compare the full distribution of loan amounts across demographic facets, rather than only group sizes or an aggregate positive-outcome rate.
Class imbalance measures how many samples belong to each facet. It does not measure how loan amounts are distributed within those facets.
Conditional demographic disparity compares outcome proportions while accounting for subgroups. It is not a direct distance between the full loan-amount distributions.
Difference in proportions of labels summarizes an outcome-rate or continuous-label difference. It does not capture all changes in distribution shape as the selected distance metrics do.
Jensen-Shannon divergence compares each facet's outcome distribution with their mixture, providing a symmetric measure of distributional difference.
Kullback-Leibler divergence measures how one facet's loan-amount distribution differs from another. It is directional and requires care where probabilities are zero.
Total variation distance aggregates probability differences across the outcome distributions, making it useful for comparing loan-amount distributions between facets.
228: CNN-QR supported item metadata and historical covariates without requiring those covariates across the entire future horizon. An upper quantile reflects a greater penalty for underforecasting.
P75 is directionally appropriate for costly stockouts, but ARIMA does not exploit item metadata and cross-item learning as the proposed CNN-QR model does.
ARIMA does not meet the metadata-related modeling needs as well, and WAPE does not express the asymmetric cost of stockouts versus excess inventory.

CNN-QR can use the item features and past promotion information even though the full 30-day promotion schedule is unavailable. P75 weighted quantile loss favors avoiding underforecasts; the ideal quantile still depends on the actual cost ratio.

CNN-QR is suitable for the available features, but WAPE penalizes absolute errors without expressing the higher cost of underpredicting demand. Forecast is a historical choice for customers without existing access.
229: Secure distributed training combines private data access, authorized inter-instance communication, and encryption of traffic exchanged among training containers.
Private VPC networking controls connectivity, while inter-container traffic encryption protects data exchanged between the eight training instances.
Splitting a training job across multiple VPCs and adding peering does not itself encrypt its traffic and is not the normal single-job VPC configuration.
An S3 VPC endpoint with appropriate routes and policies provides controlled private access to the training data without an internet route.
Read-only access to SageMaker resources does not grant the training execution role the specific S3 access it needs or configure secure instance-to-instance communication.
A NAT gateway enables outbound internet access. It is unnecessary for private S3 access through a VPC endpoint and does not secure distributed training traffic.
A security-group rule allowing the training instances to communicate with peers in the same group supports distributed coordination while avoiding broad inbound access.
230: Inference acceleration can improve neural-network throughput without paying for a large full-GPU host. Elastic Inference was an older implementation of this approach.
For supported PyTorch models, Elastic Inference historically added fractional GPU acceleration to a SageMaker endpoint. It is no longer an available option for new deployments.
More layers generally add inference computation. A larger training dataset may improve accuracy, but does not directly reduce the deployed model's latency.
Adding layers still increases model complexity, and reducing training data does not make the resulting architecture cheaper to execute.
A multi-GPU instance can be costly and requires a workload that uses its parallel capacity. It is not automatically the most economical way to accelerate this single model.
231: Lake Formation governs an S3 data lake using the Glue Data Catalog, with crawlers for discovery and integration with IAM and KMS for protected access.
Identifying and registering relevant lake locations places them under Lake Formation governance. Database data may first need an ingestion workflow into the lake.
Glue connects and catalogs data sources, but linking sources to Glue alone does not provide the requested central fine-grained Lake Formation permissions.
Glue crawlers discover schemas and populate the shared Data Catalog, making the datasets discoverable through supported analytics tools.

IAM and storage encryption are necessary foundations, but manually managing each source's permissions does not provide Lake Formation's catalog-level fine-grained governance with the same setup effort.

Lake Formation supplies fine-grained permissions and works with KMS-encrypted lake data and catalog metadata. Encryption must be configured in the underlying supported services; registration alone does not encrypt existing objects.
Glue handles discovery and ETL, but is not the central fine-grained data-lake authorization service specified by the question.
232: Overfitting occurs when a model learns training-specific patterns that do not generalize. Regularization and reduced model capacity can limit this behavior.
Changing the shuffle seed changes sample order or the split, but does not directly constrain the model's tendency to memorize training data.
A smaller learning rate changes optimization speed and stability. It does not reliably reduce model capacity or prevent eventual overfitting.
Adding layers increases capacity and can worsen overfitting when the current network already fits training-specific noise.
L1 and L2 penalties discourage unnecessarily large weights, reducing the freedom to fit noise in the training reviews.
Dropout randomly suppresses units during training, reducing dependence on particular internal features and encouraging more robust representations.
Reducing the number of layers lowers model capacity and can improve generalization when the original architecture is too complex for the available data.
233: L1 regularization encourages sparse linear-model coefficients, combining regularization with implicit feature selection.
An L1 penalty can drive some coefficients exactly to zero, reducing the active feature set while limiting overfitting.
L2 shrinks coefficients but generally does not make them exactly zero. It addresses overfitting without directly meeting the feature-removal requirement.
Dropout is primarily a neural-network regularizer and does not directly select a smaller set of coefficients for this linear model.
More representative data may improve generalization, but it does not by itself reduce the number of input features.
234: High overall accuracy can conceal weak minority-class recall. Training-only minority oversampling is one way to improve attention to rare fraud examples.
SMOTE increases the representation of minority fraud cases through synthetic training examples. Recall, precision, and false-positive costs must then be evaluated on an untouched validation set.
Oversampling the majority fair-transaction class increases the imbalance and does not address the 30% of fraud cases being missed.
Removing minority fraud cases leaves even less information about fraudulent patterns and makes the imbalance worse.
Adding more majority examples increases the dominance of fair transactions rather than improving representation of the fraud class.
235: FastFile exposes S3 training data through a file interface and retrieves content on demand, avoiding a complete local download before training starts.
File mode downloads the full input before training. For 200 TB, that creates substantial startup delay and local-storage requirements.
FSx for Lustre can deliver high throughput, especially for repeated workloads, but requires a file system and networking setup beyond selecting FastFile mode.
EFS requires provisioning, mounting, and making the S3 dataset available in the file system. It adds setup without the direct on-demand S3 integration requested.
FastFile starts reading the existing large S3 files as training needs them, minimizing setup and avoiding a full 200 TB staging step. Actual throughput still depends on the access pattern.
236: Quantile bins divide a skewed numeric feature into intervals with roughly comparable sample counts, allowing different effects in different value ranges.
One-hot encoding raw continuous durations can create many sparse categories. Binning first provides a more useful representation of a skewed numeric relationship.
A Cartesian-product transformation models interactions among categorical values. It does not directly address the skewed nonlinear effect of this single numeric feature.

Quantile binning can represent a piecewise relationship between duration and sales instead of forcing one slope across the entire range. The binned features need suitable encoding for the linear model.
Normalization changes scale but preserves the basic shape of the relationship. A nonlinear association remains nonlinear after ordinary rescaling.
237: IAM groups receive identity-based policies; they are not valid principals in S3 bucket policies or S3 ACL grants.
S3 ACLs cannot grant permissions to an IAM user group. Separate buckets do not fix the unsupported grant target.
An IAM group cannot be named as the Principal in a bucket policy. Access for its members should be granted through an identity policy attached to the group.

Group-attached policies can grant Finance access to both object prefixes and the other groups access only to the nonsensitive prefix. Relevant bucket-list permissions and any other policies must also respect those boundaries.
A bucket policy cannot directly designate the Finance IAM group as its principal, even when the data is separated into prefixes.
238: Kinesis Video Streams ingests and retains timestamp-indexed video, and HLS playback lets viewers consume the stream through compatible players.
Rekognition performs video analysis such as detection. It is not the playback interface the security team needs to watch the camera feed.
Kinesis Video Streams provides the ingestion, retention, and indexed retrieval, while its HLS capability supports viewing without building a separate video-delivery system.
Rekognition is an analysis service, and Kinesis Data Streams is not a video fragment store with the requested indexing and playback capabilities.
Firehose delivers buffered records to data destinations. It does not supply Kinesis Video Streams' video indexing and HLS playback.
239: Visual defect detection needs an image model, and review by internal employees requires a private human-review workforce. The A2I portion is a historical availability consideration.
Textract extracts document text and structure, rather than learning arbitrary plaque defects. Mechanical Turk also uses an external workforce instead of the required internal team.
A suitable Rekognition model, such as Custom Labels trained for the defect classes, can flag images. A custom A2I review workflow with a private workforce can route uncertain cases to employees.
Transcribe converts speech to text and cannot classify visual plaque defects, even though the private-workforce choice is appropriate.
Panorama targeted edge computer vision rather than this S3 image workflow, and Mechanical Turk does not restrict review to the internal team.
240: Windowed stream processing computes rolling features before writing them to the Feature Store online store for low-latency retrieval.
Firehose buffering and a Processing batch introduce delay before feature updates. They are less suitable than continuous windowed processing for near-real-time rolling averages.
GetRecord retrieves a stored feature record. It does not calculate rolling averages over historical stream events inside Feature Store.

Historically, a Kinesis SQL application could calculate the rolling window and Lambda could write the result to the online store. The retired SQL service must be replaced with a supported stream processor in a new implementation.
The offline store is designed for analytical and training access, not near-real-time online feature serving. Computing each rolling average at query time also adds latency.
